Definitions/Def_friedmann_simplex.lean.readback:
**LP.** For any natural numbers $m,n$, including zero, a rational linear-program datum consists of an $m\times n$ rational matrix $A$, a rational vector $b$ indexed by $\{0,\ldots,m-1\}$, and a rational vector $c$ indexed by $\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$; the structure itself imposes no feasibility, rank, sign, or boundedness conditions.

**Basis.** For any natural numbers $m,n$, a basis is any function $B:\{0,\ldots,m-1\}\to\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$. Injectivity and invertibility are not part of this definition. If $m=0$ the function is the empty function; if $m>0$ and $n=0$ no such function exists.

**basisMatrix.** Given natural numbers $m,n$, rational data $P=(A,b,c)$ of the indicated dimensions, and a function $B:\{0,\ldots,m-1\}\to\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$, the square matrix $M_B$ has entries $(M_B)_{ij}=A_{i,B(j)}$, so its columns are selected in the order specified by $B$, with repetitions allowed.

**basicValues.** Given natural numbers $m,n$, rational data $(A,b,c)$, and a column-selection function $B$, the basic-value vector is $u_B=M_B^{-1}b$, where $(M_B)_{ij}=A_{i,B(j)}$. This uses the total matrix inverse: a singular rational matrix has inverse the zero matrix, so the expression is defined without an invertibility hypothesis.

**basicPoint.** Given natural numbers $m,n$, rational data $(A,b,c)$, and a column-selection function $B$, put $M_{B,ij}=A_{i,B(j)}$ and $u_B=M_B^{-1}b$ using the total inverse. The vector $x_B\in\mathbb Q^n$ is defined by $(x_B)_j=\sum_{i=0}^{m-1}\mathbf1_{B(i)=j}(u_B)_i$. Repeated selections add their basic values; an unselected column receives zero; an empty sum is zero.

**feasible.** For any natural dimensions $m,n$, rational data $(A,b,c)$, and rational vector $x\in\mathbb Q^n$, feasibility means exactly $Ax=b$ and $x_j\ge0$ for every $j<n$. Zero dimensions are included, with their corresponding empty equations or coordinate conditions.

**basicFeasible.** For any natural dimensions $m,n$, rational data $(A,b,c)$, and function $B:\{0,\ldots,m-1\}\to\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$, basic feasibility means that $B$ is injective, the matrix $M_{B,ij}=A_{i,B(j)}$ has nonzero determinant, and every coordinate of $M_B^{-1}b$ is nonnegative. No additional equation about the embedded vector is included in this predicate; when $m=0$, the determinant is the empty determinant $1$ and the coordinate condition is empty.

**objective.** For natural dimensions $m,n$, rational data $(A,b,c)$, and $x\in\mathbb Q^n$, the objective is $f(x)=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}c_jx_j$, equal to zero when $n=0$.

**basicObjective.** For natural dimensions $m,n$, rational data $(A,b,c)$, and a column-selection function $B$, the basic objective is $\sum_{j<n}c_j\sum_{i<m}\mathbf1_{B(i)=j}(M_B^{-1}b)_i$, with $M_{B,ij}=A_{i,B(j)}$ and the total inverse, so it is defined even when $B$ is repeated or $M_B$ is singular.

**direction.** For natural dimensions $m,n$, rational data $(A,b,c)$, a column-selection function $B$, and $j<n$, the direction is $d_{B,j}=M_B^{-1}A_{\cdot j}$, with $M_{B,ir}=A_{i,B(r)}$ and total matrix inverse. It is defined without basic feasibility or invertibility assumptions.

**reducedCost.** For natural dimensions $m,n$, rational data $(A,b,c)$, a column-selection function $B$, and $j<n$, the reduced cost is $\bar c_{B,j}=c_j-\sum_{i<m}c_{B(i)}(M_B^{-1}A_{\cdot j})_i$, where $M_{B,ir}=A_{i,B(r)}$ and the inverse is total.

**improving.** For natural dimensions $m,n$, rational data $(A,b,c)$, a column-selection function $B$, and $j<n$, improvement means both $B(i)\ne j$ for every $i<m$ and $c_j-\sum_{i<m}c_{B(i)}(M_B^{-1}A_{\cdot j})_i>0$, with $M_{B,ir}=A_{i,B(r)}$. It does not itself require $B$ to be basic feasible.

**leaving.** For natural dimensions $m,n$, rational data $(A,b,c)$, a column-selection function $B$, an entering column $j<n$, and a row $\ell<m$, let $u=M_B^{-1}b$ and $d=M_B^{-1}A_{\cdot j}$. Row $\ell$ is leaving exactly when $d_\ell>0$ and, for every $i<m$ with $d_i>0$, $u_\ell/d_\ell\le u_i/d_i$. Ties are permitted. The predicate includes no basic feasibility or entering-improvement requirement. All inverses and rational divisions are total; the displayed denominator comparisons are restricted to positive directions.

**pivot.** For natural dimensions $m,n$, rational data $(A,b,c)$, column-selection functions $B,B'$, and $j<n$, a pivot means that $B$ is injective, $M_B$ is nonsingular and $u=M_B^{-1}b\ge0$; that $j$ is outside the image of $B$ and has positive reduced cost $c_j-\sum_{i<m}c_{B(i)}d_i$ for $d=M_B^{-1}A_{\cdot j}$; and that some row $\ell<m$ satisfies $d_\ell>0$ and $u_\ell/d_\ell\le u_i/d_i$ for every positive $d_i$, with $B'$ obtained by replacing only $B(\ell)$ by $j$ and $B'$ also injective with nonsingular selected matrix and nonnegative basic values. The choice among tied leaving rows is unrestricted.

**optimalBasis.** For natural dimensions $m,n$ and rational data $(A,b,c)$, a function $B$ is an optimal basis exactly when it is injective, $M_B$ is nonsingular, $M_B^{-1}b\ge0$, and no column outside its image has positive reduced cost $c_j-\sum_{i<m}c_{B(i)}(M_B^{-1}A_{\cdot j})_i$. This is the literal stopping predicate; it contains no separate universal comparison with all feasible objective values.

**nondegenerate.** For natural dimensions $m,n$ and rational data $(A,b,c)$, nondegeneracy means that, for every injective column-selection function $B$ whose selected matrix $M_B$ is nonsingular and whose vector $M_B^{-1}b$ is coordinatewise nonnegative, every coordinate of that vector is strictly positive. If no basic feasible $B$ exists the condition holds vacuously; if $m=0$ its concluding coordinate condition is empty.

**bounded.** For natural dimensions $m,n$ and rational data $(A,b,c)$, boundedness means that some rational number $R$ satisfies $|x_j|\le R$ for every rational vector $x$ with $Ax=b$ and $x\ge0$ and every $j<n$. The witness $R$ is not required to be nonnegative; empty feasible sets and empty coordinate sets are included.

**cyclicDistance.** For a natural number $n$, a permutation $\rho$ of $\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$, and indices $\ell,j<n$, the cyclic distance is the natural number $D_\rho(\ell,j)=((\rho(j)+n-\ell)\bmod n)$, where indices are read as their numerical values and subtraction is natural-number subtraction. The stored $\ell$ is used directly as a rank, without applying $\rho$ to it. Distance zero is included in the scan. When $n=0$ there are no arguments $\ell,j$.

**cunninghamChoice.** For natural dimensions $m,n$, rational data $(A,b,c)$, a permutation $\rho$ of the columns, a column-selection function $B$, a stored rank $\ell<n$, and a column $j<n$, choice means that $j$ lies outside the image of $B$, has positive reduced cost $c_j-\sum_{i<m}c_{B(i)}(M_B^{-1}A_{\cdot j})_i$, and minimizes $((\rho(j)+n-\ell)\bmod n)$ weakly over all columns satisfying those same two improvement conditions. It does not itself require basic feasibility; no improving column means that no choice exists.

**State.** For any natural dimensions $m,n$, a state consists of a column-selection function $B:\{0,\ldots,m-1\}\to\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$ and a stored rank $\ell<n$. No feasibility or rank conditions are fields. In particular there are no states if $n=0$.

**cunninghamStep.** For natural dimensions $m,n$, rational data $(A,b,c)$, a column permutation $\rho$, and states $(B,\ell),(B',\ell')$, a step means that some nonbasic column $j$ with positive reduced cost has weakly least distance $((\rho(j)+n-\ell)\bmod n)$ among all such columns; that $B,B'$ are both basic feasible and $B'$ is obtained from $B$ by entering $j$ and leaving a row minimizing the nonnegative-basic-value to positive-direction ratio; and that $\ell'=\rho(j)$. Ties in the ratio test are permitted.

**cunninghamRun.** For natural dimensions $m,n$, rational data $(A,b,c)$, a column permutation $\rho$, a sequence of states $(B_t,\ell_t)$ indexed by all natural numbers, and $T\in\mathbb N$, a run means that $B_0$ is basic feasible; for every $0\le t<T$, some improving nonbasic column of least cyclic distance from $\ell_t$ is entered by an actual ratio-test pivot to a basic feasible $B_{t+1}$ and $\ell_{t+1}$ is its $\rho$-rank; and $B_T$ is basic feasible with no improving nonbasic column. Here basic feasibility requires injectivity, nonzero selected determinant and nonnegative basic values, directions and reduced costs use the selected inverse, and a leaving row has positive direction and least basic-value/direction ratio. The number $T$ counts pivots, may be zero, and imposes no conditions on states after $T$, no prescribed initial basis or initial rank, and no explicit strict increase of the objective.

**Game.** For any type $V$, a game is a triple of functions assigning to each $v\in V$ an owner in $\{\mathrm{false},\mathrm{true}\}$ and a natural-number priority, together with an edge relation on $V$. The structure alone requires neither a finite vertex set nor outgoing edges nor distinct priorities.

**WellFormed.** For any type $V$, a game $G$ is well formed exactly when every vertex has an outgoing edge and the priority function is injective. Both requirements are empty when $V$ is empty.

**Legal.** For any type $V$, a game $G$, a Boolean player $b$, and a total function $\sigma:V\to V$, legality means that $G$ has an edge from $v$ to $\sigma(v)$ for every vertex $v$ whose owner is $b$. Values of $\sigma$ at the other player's vertices are unrestricted. No well-formedness assumption is imposed.

**play.** For any type $V$, a game $G$, total functions $\sigma,\tau:V\to V$, and a vertex $v$, the play at time $t\in\mathbb N$ is the $t$-fold iterate at $v$ of the function choosing $\sigma(w)$ at false-owned vertices and $\tau(w)$ at true-owned vertices. Time zero is $v$. The definition does not require either function to follow game edges.

**recurring.** For a finite type $V$ and any sequence $\pi:\mathbb N\to V$, the recurring set is $\{v\in V:\forall t\in\mathbb N,\ \exists k\in\mathbb N,\ k\ge t\ \text{and}\ \pi_k=v\}$, represented as a finite set.

**Valuation.** For any type $V$, a valuation is an unconstrained triple $(p,S,k)$ consisting of a natural-number cycle priority $p$, a finite set $S$ of vertices of type $V$, and a natural-number length $k$. The fields are not required to arise from an actual play.

**playValue.** For a finite type $V$ with decidable equality, a game $G$, total functions $\sigma,\tau:V\to V$, and $v\in V$, For strategies $\sigma,\tau:V\to V$ and a start $v$, the play is $\pi_t=F^t(v)$, where $F(w)=\sigma(w)$ when the owner is false and $F(w)=\tau(w)$ otherwise. Let $R$ be the set of vertices occurring at arbitrarily late times and $p=\max\{\operatorname{priority}(w):w\in R\}$, with empty maximum $0$. Choose an arbitrary vertex $w\in R$ of priority $p$ if one exists, and otherwise set $w=v$. Let $k$ be the least time with $\pi_k=w$, with fallback $k=0$ if that vertex never occurs. The play valuation is $(p,S,k)$, where $S=\{\pi_t:0\le t<k,\ \operatorname{priority}(\pi_t)>p\}$ is a set, so repeated visits are collapsed. No legality or injectivity assumption is imposed. If $V$ is empty there is no start $v$; all fallback conventions remain part of the total definition.

**reward.** For every natural number $p$, the integer reward is $p$ when $p$ is even and $-p$ otherwise; in particular the reward of zero is zero.

**SetLT.** For a type $V$ with decidable equality, a game $G$, and finite sets $A,B\subseteq V$, $A$ is less than $B$ exactly when there is $w\in A\mathbin{\triangle}B$ such that every $u\in A\mathbin{\triangle}B$ has priority at most the priority of $w$, and either the priority of $w$ is even and $w\in B$, or it is odd and $w\in A$. Empty symmetric difference makes the predicate false. The definition permits tied maximal priorities and does not require the game's priorities to be injective.

**ValueLT.** For a type $V$ with decidable equality, a game $G$, and arbitrary valuation triples $a,b$, Write $r(p)=p$ for even $p$ and $r(p)=-p$ for odd $p$. For triples $a=(p,A,k)$ and $b=(q,B,l)$, write $a<_{\mathrm v}b$ when either $r(p)<r(q)$; or $p=q$ and some vertex $w$ in the symmetric difference $A\mathbin{\triangle}B$ has priority at least that of every vertex in that symmetric difference and is in $B$ with even priority or in $A$ with odd priority; or $p=q$, $A=B$, and either $p$ is odd and $k<l$, or $p$ is even and $l<k$. Write $a\le_{\mathrm v}b$ for $a=b$ or $a<_{\mathrm v}b$. The predicate being defined here is precisely the strict comparison $<_{\mathrm v}$; neither valuation needs to be realized by a play and the game need not have injective priorities.

These two targets are exactly the successors at each decision vertex. The successors of $f_1$ are $h_1,e_1$, those of $f_i$ for $i>1$ are $h_i,d_i,e_i$, those of $g_i$ are just $f_i$, those of $h_i$ are just $a_{i+1}$, those of $s$ are just $c_n$, and those of $z$ are just $z$. Priorities are $3$ at decision vertices of kinds $a,b,c$, $5$ at kinds $d,e$, $6$ at every $f_i$, $2i+7$ at $g_i$, $2i+8$ at $h_i$, $8$ at $s$ and $1$ at $z$. A strategy is a total vertex-to-vertex function; legality for a player constrains it only to follow an edge at that player's vertices. For strategies $\sigma,\tau:V\to V$ and a start $v$, the play is $\pi_t=F^t(v)$, where $F(w)=\sigma(w)$ when the owner is false and $F(w)=\tau(w)$ otherwise. Let $R$ be the set of vertices occurring at arbitrarily late times and $p=\max\{\operatorname{priority}(w):w\in R\}$, with empty maximum $0$. Choose an arbitrary vertex $w\in R$ of priority $p$ if one exists, and otherwise set $w=v$. Let $k$ be the least time with $\pi_k=w$, with fallback $k=0$ if that vertex never occurs. The play valuation is $(p,S,k)$, where $S=\{\pi_t:0\le t<k,\ \operatorname{priority}(\pi_t)>p\}$ is a set, so repeated visits are collapsed. Write $N_S(p)=|\{w\in S:\operatorname{priority}(w)=p\}|$ and $r(p)=p$ for even $p$, $r(p)=-p$ for odd $p$. A set $A$ is less than a set $B$ if there is a priority $p$ with unequal counts, equal counts at every larger priority, and either $p$ even with $N_A(p)<N_B(p)$ or $p$ odd with $N_B(p)<N_A(p)$. Triples $(p,A,k)$ and $(q,B,l)$ are strictly compared by: $r(p)<r(q)$, or $p=q$ and the preceding strict set comparison, or $p=q$ and equal counts at every priority and either $p$ odd with $k<l$ or $p$ even with $l<k$. Their weak comparison means that the reverse strict comparison does not hold. The conclusion is that there exists a single total strategy function $\tau$ following an edge at every true-owned vertex such that, for every starting vertex $v$ and every true-player legal total function $\tau'$, the play valuation for $(\sigma,\tau',v)$ is not strictly below the play valuation for $(\sigma,\tau,v)$ in this multiplicity comparison. Thus one legal $\tau$ simultaneously satisfies the weak minimum condition at all starts, with weak comparison defined as absence of a reverse strict comparison rather than equality of path sets.
